abstract: Animals use both private information acquired through experience and social information produced by conspecifics when making behavioural decisions. The combination of sensory cues and their associated reward value may influence how animals weigh private information against social information. We investigated information use during foraging in the ant Pristomyrmex punctatus using Y-maze experiments with learned visual and olfactory cues and trail pheromones. Workers learned both types of private cue and showed no significant preference between them when they were placed in conflict. When private information conflicted with a high-concentration pheromone trail, workers preferred the pheromone-marked route following visual, olfactory or multimodal training. At a lower pheromone concentration, route choice depended on training modality: workers trained with either unimodal cue preferred the pheromone trail, whereas workers trained with multimodal cues (combined visual and olfactory cues) showed no significant preference between the routes. When learned visual and olfactory cues were placed in conflict, workers favoured the cue paired with the higher sucrose concentration under both reciprocal reward assignments. In contrast, workers still preferred a pheromone trail when it had been associated with a lower-quality reward than the competing multimodal cues. These results show that ants adjust their use of learned private information according to expected reward and suggest that multimodal private information can influence the balance between private and social information during foraging.
